text: For a smallholder farmer in Preah Vihear, recognizing illness across cattle, pigs, chickens, and ducks starts with knowing what is normal for each animal and checking regularly rather than waiting until an animal is severely sick. Observe appetite, water consumption, movement, breathing, behavior, body condition, manure/droppings, and production (eggs, milk, growth). Warning signs include separating from the group, weakness, unusual aggression or depression, difficulty standing/walking, coughing, sneezing, discharge, rapid/difficult breathing, diarrhea, vomiting, skin lesions, weight loss, reproductive problems, or an unexpected drop in production. During the wet season (roughly May–October), pay particular attention to wet/muddy housing, contaminated water, parasites, and humidity; during the dry season (roughly November–April), heat stress, dehydration, dust, and reduced feed availability can cause signs that resemble disease. These observations are warning signs, not diagnoses — many diseases have overlapping symptoms, and heat stress, poor nutrition, toxins, injury, parasites, or poor housing can produce similar signs. A simple notebook is sufficient: record date, animal type, number affected, key signs, deaths, recent purchases/movements, feed changes, vaccination info, and unusual weather/housing conditions. Seek veterinary or appropriate animal-health assistance promptly for sudden unexplained mortality, rapidly increasing sick animals, severe breathing difficulty, widespread neurological signs, severe diarrhea affecting many animals, hemorrhagic signs, multiple abortions, or severe group-wide weakness. No breed or variety is assumed from location alone — record the farmer's actual animal type.
